concepts.title: Periodic and Oscillatory Motion
concepts.definition: A motion that repeats itself at fixed intervals is periodic, and when the repetition happens back and forth about a mean position it is oscillatory. One full cycle takes the period T, its reciprocal is the frequency in hertz, and circular motion projected on a diameter furnishes the standard picture of such vibration.
concepts.key_idea: Repetition defines periodicity; the back-and-forth flavour about a centre defines oscillation.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 20-110 (sections 13.1, 13.2 periodic and oscillatory motions, period, frequency, displacement as function of time)

solution_steps.explain: A motion is periodic when its state repeats after a fixed, definite interval -- the period.
Oscillatory motion is periodic motion swinging either side of an equilibrium point.
Frequency counts cycles per second, the reciprocal of the period in seconds.

concepts.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: Displacement and Phase
concepts.definition: Simple harmonic motion is the ideal oscillation whose displacement varies sinusoidally with time: x equals A sin of (omega t plus phi). Here A is the amplitude -- the largest swing -- omega the angular frequency, and the phase inside tells exactly where in the cycle the oscillator sits at t = 0.
concepts.key_idea: Displacement rides a sine wave -- amplitude sets the swing size, phase sets the head start.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 111-220 (sections 13.3, 13.4 simple harmonic motion and uniform circular motion, amplitude, phase, reference circle)

solution_steps.explain: A point circling uniformly casts on a diameter a shadow that moves sinusoidally -- the reference circle picture of SHM.
The circle's radius is the amplitude, the angular speed becomes omega, and the starting angle is the initial phase.
Phase multiples of pi over two mark the mean and extreme positions, fixing when the oscillator passes them.

concepts.title: Velocity and Acceleration in SHM
concepts.definition: Differentiating the sinusoidal displacement gives the SHM velocity, omega times the square root of amplitude squared minus displacement squared, peaking at the mean position and dying at the extremes. Acceleration always points back toward the mean with size omega squared times displacement -- the defining property of simple harmonic motion.
concepts.key_idea: Acceleration proportional to displacement and opposite in sign -- that feedback loop is SHM's signature.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 221-330 (sections 13.5 velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion, 13.6 force law, maxima at mean and extreme positions)

solution_steps.explain: The magnitude of the restoring acceleration is omega squared times the displacement.

concepts.title: Period of a Spring-Block Oscillator
concepts.definition: A mass on a spring obeys Hooke's restoring force exactly, so its motion is simple harmonic with period two pi times the square root of mass over spring constant. A stiffer spring shortens the period; a heavier block lengthens it -- and neither depends on how far the mass is pulled.
concepts.key_idea: Mass over stiffness under a square root times two pi -- the isochronous clock of the spring.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 300-420 (section 13.6 force law and period of oscillation of a spring, restoring force F = -kx)

solution_steps.action: form the mass to stiffness ratio
solution_steps.explain: The period depends on the square root of mass divided by the spring constant.
Multiplying the root by two pi gives the period in seconds.

concepts.title: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
concepts.definition: An SHM oscillator shuttles energy between kinetic form at the mean position and potential form at the extremes, while the total stays fixed at half the spring constant times amplitude squared -- or equivalently half mass times omega squared times amplitude squared. The share between the forms depends only on where the oscillator is in its swing.
concepts.key_idea: Kinetic plus potential stays constant in SHM -- the amplitude alone fixes the total energy.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 421-540 (section 13.7 energy in simple harmonic motion, kinetic and potential energies, energy vs displacement graphs)

solution_steps.explain: The total energy grows with the square of the amplitude.
Half the spring constant times the squared amplitude is the constant total energy.

concepts.title: The Simple Pendulum
concepts.definition: A bob on a light string swinging through small angles is the classic oscillator: the restoring push grows from gravity's tangential component, and the motion is simple harmonic with period two pi times the square root of length over gravity. The period ignores the bob's mass and, for small swings, the amplitude too.
concepts.key_idea: Small-angle pendulum clocks depend only on length and g -- lengthen the string, slow the tick.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph206.txt lines 541-640 (section 13.8 the simple pendulum, small angle approximation, time period expression, seconds pendulum)

solution_steps.action: form the length to gravity ratio
solution_steps.explain: The pendulum period uses the square root of string length over g.
Two pi times that root is the swing period.
